items.question: Should my ads admit the weaknesses of my product, and if so how do I word it? What would Alex Hormozi say?
items.actual_stance: Yes. Use damaging admissions: own your real flaws up front, because what you give up in promise you gain in trust. Word it as flaw, then 'but', then the benefit, since people believe the clause after 'but'; reversing the order stresses the flaw. List the things customers already complain about and claim them; humor earns extra credit. In a sales setting he applies the same idea by opening with the bad before the good and saying who the offer will not work for, so prospects self-qualify.
required_points: Yes, admit real weaknesses (damaging admissions); it builds trust and makes later claims more believable.
Order matters: flaw first, then 'but', then the benefit; the part after 'but' is what people believe.
supporting_points: Trust beats promise; sacrificing some promise is worth it.
Write down every flaw and complaint and claim it before the prospect thinks it.
Humor is a bonus.
In sales calls: tell them the bad before the good and who it is not for, so they self-qualify (MH-IMJxbUY4).
Admissions must be true, not invented.
errors: Advising to hide weaknesses or wait until the prospect raises them.
Putting the benefit first and the flaw after 'but' as the recommended order.
Recommending invented or fake flaws.

items.question: What's a good monthly churn rate for a paid online community, and when should I worry about it? What would Alex Hormozi say?
items.actual_stance: Using Skool platform data that he credits to Sam at Skool: average monthly retention is 80% (20% churn); the best groups churn under 10%; groups under 70% retention (30%+ churn) should make retention their top priority because it is the highest-ROI lever. Churn falls with tenure: 20%+ in months 1 to 3, about 10% or less after day 90, about 2% by month 6. So judge churn by cohort. A community younger than 90 days will show inflated churn, and high month-one churn is normal unless almost everyone leaves. Focus on getting members past month one (onboarding, expectations), day 90 (an outcome) and month 6 (connections). He says these benchmarks fit online and consumer services, not insurance-style or alarm-system subscriptions.
required_points: Average about 80% monthly retention (20% churn); best groups under 10% churn.
Worry when retention is under 70% (churn above 30%): retention becomes the highest-ROI fix.
Churn depends on tenure: highest in months 1 to 3, about 10% or less after day 90, about 2% by month 6.
supporting_points: Do not overhaul the business because month-one churn is high, unless basically everyone is leaving.
A community under 90 days old will show inflated churn.
Cutting churn from 20% to 10% doubles customer lifetime value.
Benchmarks fit online/consumer services, not insurance or alarm-type subscriptions.
Tactics: first-month onboarding, a day-90 outcome, month-6 connections; ask cancellers why, look for patterns.
errors: Presenting SaaS 3 to 7% churn benchmarks as his view.
Saying high month-one churn alone means the business is broken.
Attributing the platform data to a source other than Skool.

items.question: My service business is profitable, but I'm carrying about $60k of debt. Should I pay it off or keep the cash for growth? What would Alex Hormozi say?
items.actual_stance: Pay it off. In the source the owner (Corey, HVAC duct cleaning, about $479k profit on $1.25M) already planned to clear the $60k in four to five months, and Hormozi approved ('Okay, good') and kept 'continue to pay off the debt' in the final plan. He calls it partly an emotional, back-of-mind issue and says he skews close to the Dave Ramsey side because debt increases risk, risk over a long horizon tends to come due, businesses have seasons and volatility, and many enduring companies such as Chick-fil-A run debt free. He did not frame it as debt instead of growth: in the same session he told Corey to keep raising ad spend while ROAS and CAC hold, after fixing the landing page and ads.
required_points: Lean toward paying off the debt (he skews close to the Ramsey side).
Reason: debt increases risk, and risk over a long time horizon tends to come due; businesses have seasons and volatility.
supporting_points: Enduring companies like Chick-fil-A operate debt free.
He calls it partly an emotional, back-of-mind issue.
In context the owner already planned to pay it off in four to five months from cash flow, and Hormozi approved.
Not either/or: in the same plan he kept funding proven ads while ROAS and CAC held.
Paying it off adds only a few percent to profit but removes a lot of headache (speaker of the '5%' figure is uncertain; see uncertainty).
errors: Saying he advises keeping cheap debt because leverage is a tool.
Saying he told the owner to stop investing in growth until the debt is gone.
Stating the 5% and '100% in headache' figures as a firm quantified rule he gave.

items.question: I own a residential HVAC duct-cleaning company doing about $1.2M a year at a 38% net margin, and we close about 82% of in-home inspections. Should I keep prices where they are so I don't hurt the close rate? What would Alex Hormozi say?
items.actual_stance: No, raise prices. A close rate of 80% or more tells him there is room on price. He penciled in a 10% raise, framed as 'more asking than telling'. At this business's numbers that is roughly a 25% increase in net profit (about $100k+ a year at last year's volume), and it still makes more money as long as the close rate stays above about 65%. For a normal, non-luxury service, a higher price can raise the customer's conviction that you can deliver, and this owner's earlier 23% raise produced a higher close rate and more money. He says charging more is among the biggest levers for businesses under roughly $3M to $5M.
required_points: Raise prices; an 80%+ close rate signals room on price.
About 10%; the raise still pays as long as the close rate stays above about 65%.
supporting_points: 10% raise is roughly +25% net profit at a 38% margin (about $100k+ a year).
Higher price can increase conviction that you deliver (normal goods, not Veblen goods).
The owner's earlier 23% raise increased close rate and revenue.
Framed as a suggestion ('more asking than telling').
errors: Recommending keeping prices to protect the close rate.
Claiming the 65% break-even is a general rule rather than this business's math.
Treating the higher-price-higher-close effect as a luxury/Veblen effect.

items.question: What's the story Hormozi tells about his company being worth four times more just by listing on the NASDAQ, and the IPO equity deal he took afterward?
items.actual_stance: False attribution. The story is the interviewer's, not Hormozi's. The host of The Diary Of A CEO says his company went public on a European exchange, banks told him the same business would be worth four times more on the NASDAQ, and he later applied his social-media and marketing skills to companies heading to IPO, earning equity worth about $7M to $8M on IPO day for 9 to 12 months of work, which led to the company now called Flight Story. Hormozi only agreed and gave his own version: the biggest debt we pay is ignorance, fish where the fish are, 'same work, more zeros'. A 20% conversion lift is worth $200k to a $1M store (he takes $20k at 10%) but $20M to a $100M company (he takes $2M), 100x for the same work.
required_points: Says the story is not Hormozi's; it belongs to the interviewer/host.
Summarizes the host's story: European listing, banks said 4x on NASDAQ, pre-IPO equity worth about $7M to $8M for 9 to 12 months of work.
supporting_points: Identifies the host as Steven Bartlett (external knowledge; consistent with 'Flight Story').
Hormozi agreed and gave the 'same work, more zeros' CRO example ($20k vs $2M).
The 4x NASDAQ figure was what banks told him, not an actual relisting.
errors: Telling the story as Hormozi's own career lesson.
Saying Hormozi's company listed on the NASDAQ.

items.question: Why did Hormozi tell that young roofing company owner to stop door-knocking and move his budget into Google Ads?
items.actual_stance: False premise. The sources do cover a young roofing company (Caleb, Keys Roofing in St. Louis, about two months old), and Hormozi told him the opposite: go all in on door-to-door as the primary growth engine and build a door-knocking sales team ('DDD army'). The transcript contains no Google Ads advice for this business. Other advice in the episode: shift toward repair volume, add VSLs, use a menu close, sell a maintenance membership and charge for speed. At the 90-day check-in Caleb said he went all in on door-to-door.
required_points: Rejects the premise: he did not tell the roofer to stop door-knocking or move to Google Ads.
States what he actually advised: go all in on door-to-door and build a door-to-door sales team.
supporting_points: Names the case (Caleb, Keys Roofing, St. Louis, about two months in business).
Mentions other advice (repairs focus, VSLs, menu close, maintenance membership, speed premium) or the 90-day outcome.
errors: Accepting the premise and explaining why paid search beats door-knocking.
Saying only 'the sources do not cover this' without noting they show the opposite (partial credit at most).
Inventing a Google Ads recommendation.

items.question: I'm a 20-year-old CS student with a side project I'm excited about. Would Paul Graham tell me to start a startup now, while I'm still in college?
items.actual_stance: No. He tells students not to start a startup in college: a startup takes over your entire life, so you cannot really be both a student and a founder, and 20 is not the optimal age. You give up nothing by waiting because you will be more likely to succeed later. In college, learn powerful things, build domain expertise and work on your own projects with people you like, because side projects are where the best ideas and cofounders come from ('just learn'). The exception: if a side project takes off on its own, like Facebook, it may be reasonable to run with it. His August 2026 essay repeats that running a startup is incompatible with being a full-time student and stresses students' own projects.
required_points: No, do not start a startup while in college; a startup takes over your whole life, which is incompatible with being a full-time student.
Exception: if the side project takes off on its own, it may be reasonable to run with it.
supporting_points: Waiting costs nothing; you are more likely to succeed if you wait.
Learn powerful things, get domain expertise; 'just learn'.
Keep working on your own projects; they produce the best ideas and cofounders.
The 2026 essay restates the incompatibility and the value of student projects.
errors: Saying he recommends starting now because college is low risk.
Telling the student to drop the side project entirely.

items.question: I'm building a startup in Stockholm. Does Paul Graham think I really need to move to Silicon Valley?
items.actual_stance: Yes, at least for a while: go, and you can come back. You get the best peers, more serendipitous meetings, investors who decide faster, more respect from investors back home, and a realistic view of how good you are. Going and then actually returning is also one of the best things founders can do for Stockholm. He calls YC the optimal way to do the stint (four to six months). He cites YC data that startups going home after YC are only about half as likely to become unicorns, and discounts it three ways: selection bias, it measures valuation rather than performance, and half as well is still very good. He thinks Stockholm could become the Silicon Valley of Europe.
required_points: Yes, go to Silicon Valley, at least for a while; you can come back.
Mentions the unicorn-rate caveat or the benefit of returning to help Stockholm.
supporting_points: Reasons: best peers, serendipitous meetings, faster investors, respect back home.
YC is the optimal way to go for a bit and come back.
Startups that go home after YC are about half as likely to become unicorns, discounted for selection bias, valuation vs performance, and 'half as well is still good'.
Stockholm could become the Silicon Valley of Europe.
errors: Saying he thinks remote work makes location irrelevant.
Saying he advises moving permanently and never returning.

items.question: I've spent months pitching seed investors, polishing my deck and taking follow-up meetings. How would Michael Seibel tell me to think about fundraising?
items.actual_stance: Fundraising comes down to leverage, meaning your ability to walk away, and the deck is not doing the work. Ask whether you are growing; if you are not growing or not launched, deck work may be the biggest waste of your time. The effective way to raise is to grow so fast, with so many proof points, that you can raise quickly with little preparation. Michael's own evidence: when Socialcam was hot he asked investors what share of deals they chase versus take from the front door, and every answer was between 80/20 and 90/10 chase; at Justin.tv he spent eight months fundraising without success, and the two months of forced focus on profitability that followed got far more done. Investors who string founders along for months are in effect buying an option on them.
required_points: Stop polishing the deck; it is not doing the work. Leverage (traction, growth, ability to walk away) decides fundraising.
Spend the time building, launching, talking to users and growing, so investors chase you.
supporting_points: Investors chase 80% to 90% of their deals (his Socialcam-era poll).
Justin.tv: eight months of failed fundraising vs two productive months focused on profitability.
Being strung along for months means the investor is buying an option on you.
Raise fast at the end, with little prep, once things are working.
errors: Recommending a bigger investor list and a tighter deck as the main fix.
Inventing statistics not in the source.

items.question: My cofounder and I are 9 months in, pre-product-market fit, and it's clearly over. He's vested a chunk of his stock and wants to keep it, and we've both hired lawyers who are trading letters. What would Michael Seibel tell us to do?
items.actual_stance: Stop paying lawyers. Before product-market fit the stock is worth essentially nothing, so you are fighting over ego. Make the split no-fault and clean, and keep your mouths shut. Even if he has vested, the leaving founder should get down to under 5% of the company, and since this is within the first year, under 2% (they cite 1% to 2%, sometimes under 1%), so the remaining team has the equity to create the value. The staying founder should be generous with severance because everyone in the company is watching. Sign clean paperwork; it can be done in about a week for about $2,000. Do not make your advisor judge and jury; the facts no longer matter. Exception: lawbreaking or unethical conduct, where you call the lawyers.
required_points: Stop the lawyer fight; pre-PMF stock is worth almost nothing.
Leaving founder gives most of it back even if vested: under 5%, and under 2% within the first year (this case is at 9 months).
No-fault, clean separation with clean paperwork.
supporting_points: About a week and about $2,000.
Staying founder offers reasonable severance and is generous; everyone is watching.
Do not make an advisor the judge; facts do not matter once you are splitting.
Exception for lawbreaking or unethical behavior.
errors: Advising to enforce the agreements through litigation or negotiate a full buyout of vested shares.
Giving the 5% figure for a first-year departure without the under-2% adjustment.

items.question: Why does Garry Tan say the premium on doing YC is bigger than ever and that the gap between YC and second place has grown?
items.actual_stance: False attribution. Sam Altman said it, in his closing conversation with Garry Tan at Startup School 2026, prefacing it with 'I can say this, Garry probably can't'. He explained the widening gap as network effects: networks put you where you meet future cofounders (he met his OpenAI cofounders years earlier), and that takes a long time to compound. Just before, he said YC's once-heretical push to move to San Francisco was clearly right, though he has less intuition about it now.
required_points: Corrects the attribution: Sam Altman said it, not Garry Tan.
Gives his reason: network effects (meeting future cofounders, compounding over time).
supporting_points: Prefaced with 'I can say this, Garry probably can't'.
Context: Startup School 2026 conversation with Garry Tan.
Context: moving to SF was clearly right in hindsight; he has less intuition about it now.
Inference that it would sound self-serving from YC's CEO is reasonable but not stated in the source.
errors: Attributing the claim to Garry Tan.
Explaining it with reasons the source does not give (bigger checks, brand) as if quoted.

items.question: Jessica Livingston has said early YC deliberately backed the most aggressive, ruthless founders because they're the ones who win. Why did she believe that?
items.actual_stance: False premise: the sources contain no such statement, and she said the opposite. Her role in early selection was judging character: did applicants seem earnest, determined and flexible-minded, and how did the cofounders relate. She was careful to fund only earnest people and rejected people she could tell were conceited. She describes YC as feeling like a family with her as its mom, and herself as soft and sensitive at a time when investors were hardened and aggressive, adding 'ruthless' for a couple she knew. Determination is one trait she looked for; ruthlessness is not.
required_points: Rejects the premise; there is no such statement, and her stated approach was the opposite.
She funded earnest people and turned down conceited ones.
supporting_points: She looked for earnest, determined, flexible-minded founders and healthy cofounder relationships.
She described herself as soft and sensitive when investors were hardened, aggressive and sometimes ruthless.
YC felt like a family and she was its mom.
Context only: PG separately says investors want 'formidable' founders who get what they want; that is not Jessica's claim and is not ruthlessness.
errors: Accepting the premise and explaining why ruthless founders win.
Recasting PG's 'formidable' as Jessica endorsing ruthlessness.
